health.hpsa_dh_score.plain: A priority score that the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) gives a dental shortage area. A higher score means a higher priority for sending National Health Service Corps (NHSC) clinicians.
health.hpsa_dh_score.definition: The HPSA Score of the municipality's area-level dental designation: a whole number that HRSA's National Health Service Corps (NHSC), a federal program that places clinicians in shortage areas, uses to set priorities for assigning clinicians. HRSA scores dental designations from 0 to 26 and says the higher the score, the greater the priority. HRSA builds the score by its own rules, so it is an index, not a measurement. Only area-level designations count: the municipality's low-income residents, its whole population or a high-needs area (in the 2026-10 snapshot there are 77, one for each of 77 municipalities); facility designations (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. If a municipality had more than one area designation the highest score would be shown. There is no value for Puerto Rico as a whole because scores are not added or averaged.
health.hpsa_dh_score.method: Same designations as health.hpsa_dh_short; the value is the file's HPSA Score column, as a whole number.
health.hpsa_dh_score.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot the dental scores of the 77 designated municipalities run from 14 to 26; Adjuntas, Ciales and Comerío and 16 more have the highest (26). Use it to rank municipalities within one discipline. Scores of different disciplines (primary care, dental, mental health) come from different rules and different designations, so they are not on one scale.
caveats: No value (1 municipality for dental) means HRSA's file has no area-level dental designation in force for the municipality. It is not a zero, not missing data and not proof that the municipality has enough dentists: HRSA withdrew the area designation it once had.
A score ranks priority for clinician placement. It does not measure how many people lack care, and it can change when HRSA reviews the designation.
HRSA's practitioner counts belong to each designation and are as current as its last review: the dental area designations in Puerto Rico were set between 2012 and 2023 and last updated in 2023.
health.hpsa_dh_score.geography: 78 municipalities (no value for Puerto Rico as a whole)

health.hpsa_dh_met.plain: The share of the dentists a shortage area needs that the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) counts as in place. It is not the share of people who get care.
health.hpsa_dh_met.definition: The dentists in place (full-time equivalents) divided by the practitioners in place plus those still needed, times 100, for the municipality's area-level dental designation. It is HRSA's "percent of need met" (HRSA divides the practitioners available by the number needed to bring the ratio of people to practitioners below the limit for designation), worked out here for each municipality from the file's HPSA FTE and HPSA Shortage columns. Only area-level designations count: the municipality's low-income residents, its whole population or a high-needs area (in the 2026-10 snapshot there are 77, one for each of 77 municipalities); facility designations (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the municipal FTE divided by the sum of FTE plus shortage over the designated municipalities; it leaves out the facility designations that HRSA's own figure includes, so it reads 48.2% where HRSA's figure is 48.02%.
health.hpsa_dh_met.method: Same designations as health.hpsa_dh_short. For each, need met = HPSA FTE ÷ (HPSA FTE + HPSA Shortage) × 100; there is no value when both are zero. Check against HRSA: adding the correctional facility designation to the 77 area designations gives 48.02%; HRSA's Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary (as of 30 September 2026) gives 48.02% for Puerto Rico. The populations also agree: the designation populations of the area designations (2,289,505) and the correctional facility (2,500) add up to HRSA's figure for the population of designated areas (2,292,005).
health.hpsa_dh_met.how_to_read: 100% would end the designation; 0% means HRSA counts no dentist for it. In the 2026-10 snapshot Fajardo (99.1%), Quebradillas (91.6%) and Guayama (90.0%) are the closest to ending their dental designation, and 7 of the 77 designated municipalities are at 0% (Culebra, Florida, Guánica and Guayanilla and others). Compare municipalities, not disciplines: each discipline has its own limit and its own designations.
caveats: It is the share of the practitioners that HRSA's formula needs and counts as in place. It is not the share of people who get care.

No value (1 municipality for dental) means HRSA's file has no area-level dental designation in force for the municipality. It is not a zero, not missing data and not proof that the municipality has enough dentists: HRSA withdrew the area designation it once had.

0% means HRSA counts no dentist serving the designated population, not that none works in the municipality. For a designation of a low-income population HRSA counts a practitioner's FTE from the time spent on low-income patients (Medicaid claims, or hours with Medicaid and sliding-fee patients), from hours that practitioners report in surveys run by the state primary care offices (HRSA's Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026): a practitioner who serves few such patients, or whose data HRSA does not have, adds little or nothing.

HRSA's formula counts dentists only. HRSA's practitioner counts belong to each designation and are as current as its last review: the dental area designations in Puerto Rico were set between 2012 and 2023 and last updated in 2023.
The share is the output of a federal formula. It is a good way to rank municipalities by how far each is from ending its designation, and a poor way to say how many people lack care.
health.hpsa_dh_met.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the summed practitioners in place divided by the summed practitioners needed, not an average of the municipal shares)

health.hpsa_dh_short.plain: How many more dentists a shortage area still needs for its federal shortage designation to end. The count is from the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), in full-time equivalents.
health.hpsa_dh_short.definition: The number of additional dentists, in full-time equivalents (FTE), that HRSA says the municipality's designated dental shortage area still needs for its ratio of people to practitioners to fall below the limit for designation, so that the designation would end. The limit is 5,000 people for each dentist for a whole area, and 4,000 for a low-income population group or an area of unusually high need. HRSA's file states a goal of 4,000 to 1 for all 77 designations in Puerto Rico, and its figures work out to it. HRSA counts a practitioner's FTE by its own rules, which can count a practitioner as a fraction of an FTE or as none (its Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026). Only area-level designations count: the municipality's low-income residents, its whole population or a high-needs area (in the 2026-10 snapshot there are 77, one for each of 77 municipalities); facility designations (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. The Puerto Rico value adds the municipal values.
health.hpsa_dh_short.method: health_series.py streams HRSA's dental HPSA file (BCD_HPSA_FCT_DET_DH.csv, all states and territories), keeps the Puerto Rico rows and sixteen columns, and for each municipality takes the area-level designation whose status is Designated (or Proposed For Withdrawal, which HRSA still counts until the Federal Register notice) and whose type is Geographic HPSA, HPSA Population or High Needs Geographic HPSA. In the 2026-10 snapshot that gives 77 designations and 23 facility designations are left out. The value is the file's HPSA Shortage column. If a municipality ever had two area designations the build would keep the larger shortage (the groups overlap, so they are not added) and say so in the notes of the file; a designation that covers two municipalities stops the build. Check: HRSA's own Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary (as of 30 September 2026) gives 297 dental practitioners needed for Puerto Rico; the sum of the municipal values is 296.7 and, with the correctional facility designation that HRSA includes, 298.4.
health.hpsa_dh_short.how_to_read: Read it as the size of the gap in practitioners, not in people. In the 2026-10 snapshot the largest gaps are in San Juan (15.3), Bayamón (11.5), Caguas (11.3) and Ponce (9.6); the smallest is 0.05. A large municipality needs more than a small one, so compare per 1,000 residents on the Analysis tab, or use the share of need met (health.hpsa_dh_met). 1 municipality shows no value.
caveats: No value (1 municipality for dental) means HRSA's file has no area-level dental designation in force for the municipality. It is not a zero, not missing data and not proof that the municipality has enough dentists: HRSA withdrew the area designation it once had.
HRSA's formula counts dentists only. A municipality can have care that the formula does not see.

For a designation of a low-income population HRSA counts a practitioner's FTE from the time spent on low-income patients (Medicaid claims, or hours with Medicaid and sliding-fee patients), from hours that practitioners report in surveys run by the state primary care offices (HRSA's Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026): a practitioner who serves few such patients, or whose data HRSA does not have, adds little or nothing.
HRSA's practitioner counts belong to each designation and are as current as its last review: the dental area designations in Puerto Rico were set between 2012 and 2023 and last updated in 2023.
The Puerto Rico value adds the municipal values and leaves out the facility designations, so it is a little below HRSA's own total.

Per 1,000 residents, the Puerto Rico value divides the island's total by all of the island's residents, including those of the 1 municipality with no designation (they add residents and no shortage), so it can be lower than the value of every municipality that has one.

conditions.hosp_drive_min.plain: About how many minutes it takes to drive, with no traffic, from where a barrio's people live to the nearest general hospital with an emergency room. An estimate made by the observatory.
conditions.hosp_drive_min.plain_es: Cuántos minutos, más o menos, toma ir en auto, sin tráfico, desde donde vive la gente de un barrio hasta el hospital general con sala de emergencias más cercano. Es un estimado del observatorio.
conditions.hosp_drive_min.definition: The drive time, at the observatory's free-flow planning speeds for each class of road, from a barrio's population-weighted point to the nearest general acute care hospital with emergency services in CMS's Hospital General Information list. 0 when the barrio holds a hospital. A municipio's figure is the average of its barrios weighted by 2020 residents. Vieques and Culebra have no road link to a hospital and no value.
conditions.hosp_drive_min.method: conditions.py takes CMS's general acute care hospitals with emergency services (52), places each at the OpenStreetMap hospital of its municipio with the same name (29, from gazetteer.json), else at an OpenStreetMap hospital within 1 km of HHS's geocoded address whose name shares a word with CMS's (8), else at HHS's geocoded address itself (15), and runs a shortest-path search from all of them over roads.bin in both directions of every road (care_access.py's search). Each barrio's point is the average of its 2020 census blocks' internal points weighted by residents (population_blocks.json; the barrio's internal point when no one lives there), snapped to the nearest road within 2 km that reaches a hospital. A barrio that holds a hospital is 0; which barrios those are is uncertain near the 15 hospitals placed at HHS's point (for 13 of the 27 hospitals placed by name that HHS also places, HHS's point falls in another barrio). A municipio's and Puerto Rico's figure is the average of their barrios weighted by 2020 residents, over the barrios that have a value.
conditions.hosp_drive_min.how_to_read: 10.9 minutes on average for Puerto Rico's residents with a road link; San Juan 1.9, Orocovis 37.6. The farthest barrio is Cacaos in Orocovis (48.6). 41 barrios hold a general hospital.
caveats: Free-flow speeds: no traffic, lights or stops, so real trips take longer; the road distance is the firmer figure.
A hospital point can be a few hundred metres off where OpenStreetMap or HHS placed it; HHS's points are the rougher ones.

Which barrios show 0 is uncertain near the 15 hospitals placed at HHS's geocoded address, not at their OpenStreetMap building: for 13 of the 27 hospitals placed by name that HHS also places, HHS's point falls in another barrio.
The original WCRP index measured from each barrio's centroid; this measures from where its residents live.
Vieques and Culebra have no value: the trip needs a ferry or a flight. Two uninhabited barrios (Isla de Mona, Santa Rosa in Utuado) have none either.

health.hc_drive_min.plain: A rough estimate of how many minutes residents of each municipality would drive to the nearest community health center.
health.hc_drive_min.plain_es: Un estimado aproximado de cuántos minutos manejarían los residentes de cada municipio hasta el centro de salud comunitario más cercano.
health.hc_drive_min.definition: The same search as the road distance, with the observatory's planning speed for each class of road (free flow: no traffic, no stops), averaged over the municipality's residents, in minutes.
health.hc_drive_min.method: care_access.py, run by care_series.py, searches the observatory's road graph (site/data/roads.bin, from OpenStreetMap) from every permanent health center site of HRSA's list at once, in both directions of every road, and measures from each 2020 census block with residents (its internal point, snapped to the nearest road that is joined to the network within 2 km) to the nearest site. A municipality's value is the average over its residents (each block weighted by its 2020 residents). The site points come from HRSA's file and stay in the local cache only (owner decision, 2026-10-14); they are never published. In the 2026-10 run, 124 sites, 36,570 blocks; 3 blocks (46 residents) have no road within 2 km and are left out.
health.hc_drive_min.how_to_read: About 7.4 minutes on average for Puerto Rico. Real trips are longer: the speeds assume free-flowing traffic.
caveats: It is the distance to the nearest health center (a federally funded community health center or look-alike), not to a hospital, an emergency department or a doctor's office.
It says nothing about hours, services, waiting times or whether the center takes a person's insurance.
An estimate made by the observatory, not a figure HRSA publishes.

providers.prov_dentists.plain_es: Cuántos dentistas están registrados con una dirección de práctica en cada municipio.
providers.prov_dentists.definition: Dentists registered in NPPES with a practice location in the municipio (taxonomy codes 1223). Counted at the primary practice location in the NPPES registry, by the provider's primary taxonomy code. A registry, not a head count: a provider who left, retired or works part-time may still be listed. To protect individuals, a municipio with 1 to 9 is shown empty; the island total is exact.
providers.prov_dentists.method: providers.py streams the NPPES monthly full file, keeps individual providers (entity type 1) with an active NPI and a Puerto Rico practice location, and counts them by their primary taxonomy code in the municipio of the practice location: the city when it is a municipio's name, else a known postal place, else the municipio holding most of the land of the ZIP code (the placement nonprofits.py uses; 99.9% placed). A municipio with 1 to 9 is not published.
providers.prov_dentists.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 1,773 registered; 587 of them updated their record in the last five years. The number practising is likely between the two. Most: San Juan (456), Bayamón (149), Ponce (96).
caveats: A registry, not a head count: a provider who left Puerto Rico, retired or works part-time may still be listed; one person who practises in several municipios is counted once.
To protect individuals, a municipio with 1 to 9 is shown empty; 0 and 10 or more are shown, and the island total is exact.
14,018 of the 25,740 records counted were last updated more than five years ago.

health.hc_sites.plain: How many permanent sites of community health centers are in each municipality. The list is from the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), a federal agency.
health.hc_sites.definition: Active sites in HRSA's list of Health Center Service Delivery and Look-Alike Sites that deliver care (their type is "Service Delivery Site" or "Administrative/Service Delivery Site") and whose location type is "Permanent", counted in the municipality that holds the site's county code. A federally funded health center (a Federally Qualified Health Center, FQHC) holds a federal health center grant; a look-alike meets the same requirements without the grant. Only sites whose status is "Active" are counted: HRSA uses that status for a site whose organisation has a current health center grant and that is itself open for business. The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the 78 municipal values.
health.hc_sites.method: health_series.py streams HRSA's file (all states and territories), keeps the Puerto Rico rows (Site State Abbreviation = PR) and seven of its columns, and counts, for each five-digit county code (the municipio), the rows whose status is Active, whose type delivers care and whose location type is Permanent. Of the 164 Puerto Rico rows in the 2026-11 snapshot, 120 are permanent sites that deliver care, 35 are mobile vans (health.hc_vans) and 9 are administrative-only buildings, which are left out. Names, addresses, telephone numbers, web addresses and coordinates are dropped as the file is read and are never stored or published.
health.hc_sites.how_to_read: Use it to see where the community health center sites are. In the 2026-11 snapshot San Juan has 7 permanent sites, Bayamón 7, and Mayagüez, Ponce, San Sebastián and Toa Alta 4 each; 8 municipalities have none (Añasco, Cataño, Fajardo, Guayanilla, Juana Díaz, Manatí, Sabana Grande and San Germán). On the Analysis tab the layer is shaded per 1,000 residents by default, so that a small municipality can be compared with a large one. A site is a place, not an organisation, and not a measure of care: it says nothing about hours, services, staff or how many people a site serves.
caveats: HRSA lists only health centers that hold a federal grant or look-alike status. Hospitals, private clinics, doctors' offices and the island's own public health system are not in this file.
A zero is a real zero in HRSA's list. It does not mean residents have no care nearby: a site in the next municipality, a hospital or a private clinic can serve them.
A site belongs to the municipality HRSA gives for it, which is where the site is registered.
health.hc_sites.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the sum of the 78 municipal values)

health.sites_method.plain: The sites come from the public list of the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) of health centers with a federal grant or look-alike status (a look-alike meets the same rules without the grant). The observatory counts permanent sites that deliver care, counts mobile vans apart and publishes only the counts.
health.sites_method.definition: HRSA's Health Center Service Delivery and Look-Alike Sites file lists each site of a health center that holds a federal Health Center Program grant (FQHC) or look-alike status, with the county that holds the site. A site's status says whether its organisation holds a current grant and the site is open; its type says whether it offers direct patient care, works as an administrative office or both; its location type says whether it is permanent, a mobile van, seasonal or unknown.
health.sites_method.method: (1) health_series.py downloads the file once and streams it, so the whole file is never held. (2) It keeps the rows whose Site State Abbreviation is PR and seven columns: state, status, health center type, site type, location type, the five-digit county code and the record date; names, addresses, telephone numbers, web addresses and coordinates are dropped as each row is read, so they never reach the cache. (3) A row counts when its status is Active and its type contains "Service Delivery" (a service delivery site, or an administrative and service delivery site). (4) Permanent rows are counted as hc_sites and Mobile Van rows as hc_vans, for each county code that is one of the 78 municipios; a county code that is not one stops the build. (5) A municipality with no row has a count of zero, and the Puerto Rico value is the sum.
health.sites_method.how_to_read: A count is the number of places HRSA lists, not the number of clinics (one organisation can run many sites) or the number of people served. HRSA says that, for domestic violence shelters, the building number, street and ZIP Code are removed; the observatory drops every address as each row is read, before anything is saved. The file does not say which sites accept which patients or what services they offer.
caveats: The list covers only health centers in HRSA's Health Center Program. It leaves out hospitals, private practices and the island's public health facilities.
The county code is the one HRSA registers for the site; a site on a municipal boundary is counted once, in that municipality.
health.sites_method.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the sum of the 78 municipal values)

population.acs_uninsured_pct.plain: Out of every 100 people the survey counts outside institutions, how many have no health insurance of any kind.
population.acs_uninsured_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 personas que la encuesta cuenta fuera de instituciones, cuántas no tienen seguro de salud de ningún tipo.
population.acs_uninsured_pct.definition: People with no health insurance coverage divided by the civilian population living outside institutions (table B27010: the four age groups without coverage over the total), in percent. Coverage of any kind counts: employer, direct purchase, Medicare, Medicaid or Plan Vital, military or VA.
population.acs_uninsured_pct.method: The observatory reads table B27010 (Types of Health Insurance Coverage by Age) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows, and works the value out by adding the four cells "No health insurance coverage" (017, 033, 050, 066) and dividing by the total (001). The Census Bureau does not publish this table for block groups, so there is no block-group value. The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A total that the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no margin; the observatory gives it a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done, so a share of it keeps the margin of its numerator. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give zero, which would read as exact. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.
population.acs_uninsured_pct.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 5.72% of the civilian population of Puerto Rico living outside institutions had no health insurance (margin ±0.13), against 6.82% in 2017-2021.
caveats: The windows share years: the change from one to the next is not a yearly trend.
Barrio and tract values have wide margins; the map hatches the least reliable.
population.acs_uninsured_pct.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts (not published for block groups)
population.acs_uninsured_pct.source_detail: ACS 5-year table table B27010 (Types of Health Insurance Coverage by Age), table-based summary files, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/{vintage}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ (vintages 2021 to 2024). The cells used are checked against the Census Bureau's own labels, https://api.census.gov/data/{vintage}/acs/acs5/groups/table.json, in every vintage at every build.

HRSA scores mental health designations from 0 to 25 and says the higher the score, the greater the priority. HRSA builds the score by its own rules, so it is an index, not a measurement. Only area-level designations count: the municipality's low-income residents, its whole population or a high-needs area (in the 2026-10 snapshot there are 52, one for each of 52 municipalities); facility designations (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. health.hpsa_mh_met.plain: The share of the psychiatrists a shortage area needs, by the formula of the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), that HRSA counts as in place. It is not the share of people who get care.
health.hpsa_mh_met.definition: The mental health providers (in Puerto Rico, psychiatrists) in place (full-time equivalents) divided by the practitioners in place plus those still needed, times 100, for the municipality's area-level mental health designation. The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the municipal FTE divided by the sum of FTE plus shortage over the designated municipalities; it leaves out the facility designations that HRSA's own figure includes, so it reads 8.5% where HRSA's figure is 8.31%.

health.shortage_method.plain: A Health Professional Shortage Area is a federal label, called a designation, for an area, a group of people or a facility with too few primary care, dental or mental health practitioners. The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) gives it. The observatory shows, for each municipality, the priority score, the practitioners still needed and the share of need met.
health.shortage_method.definition: HRSA designates a Health Professional Shortage Area (HPSA) when the ratio of people to practitioners passes a limit (for primary care, 3,500 to 1 for a whole area and 3,000 to 1 for a low-income population group or an area of unusually high need; for dental care, 5,000 to 1 and 4,000 to 1; for mental health, based on psychiatrists, 30,000 to 1 for a whole area and, for a low-income population group or an area of unusually high need, 20,000 to 1 or 15,000 to 1 together with 4,500 to 1 for core mental health professionals; HRSA's file states a goal of 3,000, 4,000 and 20,000 to 1 for the primary care, dental and mental health designations of Puerto Rico, and its mental health figures work out at about 15,000). A designation covers a geographic area, a population group or a facility. HRSA's "practitioners needed to remove designations" is the number of additional practitioners that its formula says would bring the ratio down to its target, and its "percent of need met" is the practitioners in place divided by the number that formula needs.
health.shortage_method.method: (1) health_series.py downloads HRSA's three files (primary care, dental health, mental health) once and streams them, keeping the Puerto Rico rows and sixteen columns without names. (2) It keeps a designation when its status is Designated or Proposed For Withdrawal (HRSA counts both) and its type is Geographic HPSA, HPSA Population or High Needs Geographic HPSA: the area-level designations. Facility designations (health centers designated by law, and one correctional facility) are left out of the municipal values. (3) A designation is assigned to the municipality of its county code; it must be the only row of its HPSA ID (one that covered two municipalities would stop the build). (4) For a municipality the score is the highest HPSA Score, the practitioners still needed is HPSA Shortage, and need met is HPSA FTE ÷ (HPSA FTE + HPSA Shortage) × 100. If a municipality ever had two area designations the larger shortage would be kept, because the groups overlap, and the file's notes would count it. (5) A municipality with no area-level designation has no value, never a zero. (6) The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the shortages and the ratio of the summed FTE to the summed FTE plus shortage; scores have no Puerto Rico value. Check against HRSA: its Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary (as of 30 September 2026) gives, for Puerto Rico, 138, 297 and 70 practitioners needed and 28.90%, 48.02% and 8.31% of need met for primary care, dental health and mental health. With the correctional facility designation added to the municipal ones, the build gets 136.8, 298.4 and 70.7 practitioners (each within 1.1%) and 28.91%, 48.02% and 8.32%, and the designation populations add up exactly to HRSA's (574,059; 2,292,005; 1,140,925).
health.shortage_method.how_to_read: In Puerto Rico every area-level designation read here is for a low-income population group (one dental designation is a high-needs geographic area), so the figures describe the shortage for those residents, as HRSA measures it, and not for every resident. Compare municipalities within one discipline. The score ranks priority, the practitioners still needed measures the gap and the share of need met shows how far a municipality is from ending its designation.
caveats: HRSA's formulas count primary care physicians only (not nurse practitioners or physician assistants), dentists only, and, for every mental health designation in Puerto Rico, psychiatrists only.
Designations are reviewed on HRSA's schedule: the area designations read here were set between 2012 and 2024 and last updated between 2016 and 2024, so a figure can be years behind the present.

The Medically Underserved Area (MUA/P) file is not used: its 72 Puerto Rico rows are all from 1978, and the underservice score, which HRSA builds from four indicators that are empty in those rows, reads 0.00 for 71 of them and 50.00 for one. The Area Health Resources File is not used because its documentation does not authorise re-use without the Bureau's permission.

community.bh_all.plain: How many treatment facilities for substance use, mental health or both each municipio has, as SAMHSA's national directories list them.
community.bh_all.plain_es: Cuántos centros de tratamiento de uso de sustancias, de salud mental o de ambos tiene cada municipio, según los directorios nacionales de SAMHSA.
community.bh_all.definition: Facilities in Puerto Rico listed in SAMHSA's National Directory of Drug and Alcohol Use Treatment Facilities or its National Directory of Mental Health Treatment Facilities (2025 editions, survey of 2024), in the municipio of their address. A facility in both directories counts once.
community.bh_all.method: community_assets.py finds the newest edition on SAMHSA's National Directories page and reads the Puerto Rico rows of its two Excel files in memory (52 in the substance use directory and 59 in the mental health directory for the 2025 edition). A facility listed in both (24) counts once: the two lists are joined on a one-way hash of the name and address. Its type of care comes from the codes SA (substance use treatment) and MH (mental health treatment) in either list. Each facility is placed in the municipio of its city (Coto Laurel is Ponce, Garrochales is Arecibo). Names, addresses and telephones are never written to disk or published.
community.bh_all.how_to_read: SAMHSA lists 87 facilities in Puerto Rico: San Juan 15, Bayamón 9, Ponce 8, Mayagüez 8. 49 municipios have none listed. The Analysis tab shows them per 1,000 residents when shaded.
caveats: Counts only. These are sensitive services, so no facility's name, address or point is published.

The directories list the facilities that answered SAMHSA's yearly survey and agreed to be listed. Facilities that did not answer, most individual practitioners and private offices are missing, so a 0 does not mean no care is offered there.
The survey describes 2024. SAMHSA's live locator (FindTreatment.gov) is more current but states no licence for reuse, so it is not used.
A facility is counted where its address is; people travel to care, often to another municipio.

community.bh_both.plain: How many facilities in each municipio treat both substance use and mental health, as SAMHSA's directories list them.
community.bh_both.plain_es: Cuántos centros de cada municipio tratan tanto el uso de sustancias como la salud mental, según los directorios de SAMHSA.
community.bh_both.definition: Facilities whose listed type of care includes both substance use treatment and mental health treatment, in either of SAMHSA's 2025 National Directories.
community.bh_both.method: community_assets.py finds the newest edition on SAMHSA's National Directories page and reads the Puerto Rico rows of its two Excel files in memory (52 in the substance use directory and 59 in the mental health directory for the 2025 edition). A facility listed in both (24) counts once: the two lists are joined on a one-way hash of the name and address. Its type of care comes from the codes SA (substance use treatment) and MH (mental health treatment) in either list. Each facility is placed in the municipio of its city (Coto Laurel is Ponce, Garrochales is Arecibo). Names, addresses and telephones are never written to disk or published.
community.bh_both.how_to_read: 42 facilities in Puerto Rico: San Juan 10; Ponce, Mayagüez and Caguas 4 each.
caveats: Counts only. These are sensitive services, so no facility's name, address or point is published.

The directories list the facilities that answered SAMHSA's yearly survey and agreed to be listed. Facilities that did not answer, most individual practitioners and private offices are missing, so a 0 does not mean no care is offered there.
The survey describes 2024. SAMHSA's live locator (FindTreatment.gov) is more current but states no licence for reuse, so it is not used.
A facility is counted where its address is; people travel to care, often to another municipio.
